title: Vendor Managed Services
overview: Map an architectural need to a managed-service category, then to a provider example. Compare compute, storage, networking, data, messaging and security across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Similar categories help comparison, but service semantics and customer responsibilities still need checking.
big_ideas: Gartner Magic Quadrants evaluate vendors on weighted criteria; AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud are the main providers compared.
Compute comes in three managed flavours: VMs (EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine), Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE) and FaaS (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions).
Storage comes as object (S3, Blob, Cloud Storage), block (EBS, Persistent Disk) and file (EFS, Azure Files, Filestore); pick by access pattern.
Networking building blocks: virtual network, DNS, load balancing and firewall, each with a managed equivalent on every major cloud.
Data services cover RDBMS, NoSQL, data warehouse, big data, AutoML and data catalogue/integration.
Messaging splits into streaming, event-driven, message queue and notification, each solving a different decoupling problem.
Monitoring, IaC, identity management and key encryption are managed too, so automation and security need not be built from scratch.

sections.title: Vendor landscape and compute
sections.summary: How Gartner evaluates cloud platform and cloud database vendors, and the three kinds of managed compute.

notes.h: Analyst reports: vendor viability, not fit
notes.lead: Gartner's Magic Quadrants weight criteria such as:
items: **Cloud platforms** → market responsiveness, overall viability, product strength
**Cloud databases** → offering strategy and innovation
notes.foot: Use them as **one input** alongside region, price and skills.

notes.h: Managed compute: three levels of control
items: **VMs (EC2)** → most control and most to operate
**Managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE)** → long-running containerised services, cross-cloud portability
**FaaS (Lambda)** → short event-driven tasks, no function servers to operate, usage-based billing

notes.lead: Providers offer overlapping building blocks, not identical semantics.
items: **First** state the capability needed

terms.def: Analyst chart placing vendors as Leaders, Challengers, Visionaries or Niche Players by ability to execute and completeness of vision.
Managed Kubernetes services on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud respectively.
Functions as a Service: run event-triggered code without managing servers.

check.q: A CIO wants to pick the provider ranked highest in an analyst's Magic Quadrant and stop there. What does the ranking tell you, and what does it not?

items: **Tells you**: an **independent view** of **vendor viability and capability**, using **weighted criteria** such as **overall viability**, **market responsiveness** and **product strength**
**Doesn't tell you**: whether the vendor **fits this workload**
**Also check**: the **regions** you need, **pricing**, your **team's skills** and how **specific services behave**
a.foot: Treat the ranking as **one input among several**.

check.q: On the same provider, a team must run (a) a long-running order API that may later move to another cloud and (b) an image-resize task triggered a few hundred times a day. Managed Kubernetes, FaaS or VMs for each?

items: **(a) Order API → managed Kubernetes**: **long-running containerised services** keep their **packaging and orchestration portable** across clouds
**(b) Image resize → FaaS**: **short**, **event-driven**, **no servers to operate**, and **billed only per use** at this volume
a.foot: **VMs** would give the **most control** but the **most to operate** → justified only if a workload needs **OS-level control**.

check.q: Two providers both list a 'managed message queue'. A teammate says they are interchangeable, so switching later will be easy. Do you agree?

a.lead: **No.** Providers offer **overlapping building blocks**, not **identical semantics**.
items: **Can differ**: **ordering**, **delivery guarantees**, **message size limits**, **access model**, **regions** and **operating boundaries**
**State the capability** you need and **check each product** against it
Keep **provider-specific calls behind your own interface** if **switching** is a real requirement

sections.title: Storage and networking
sections.summary: The three storage types and when to use each, then the managed networking services.

items: **Object (S3)** → unstructured data at scale: media, backups, archives
**Block (EBS, Persistent Disk)** → low-latency VM and database disks
**File (EFS, Filestore)** → shared file systems mounted by many VMs, often for lift-and-shift
**VPC/VNet** → logical isolation
**DNS** → naming
**Load balancing** → distributing traffic; a load balancer helps availability only when healthy backend capacity remains
**Network firewall rules** → connections
**WAF** → HTTP-level filtering

notes.lead: Managed reduces infrastructure work, not design responsibility.
items: **Select** capacity and availability options
**Configure** permissions and retention
**Test** recovery
notes.foot: A service being managed does **not by itself satisfy an application SLA**.

terms.def: Stores data as objects with metadata in a flat namespace; ideal for unstructured data at scale (S3, Blob, Cloud Storage).
Raw disk volumes attached to VMs; used for OS disks and databases (EBS, Persistent Disk).
Shared network file system mounted by many VMs (EFS, Azure Files, Filestore).
Web Application Firewall that filters malicious HTTP traffic in front of web apps.

check.q: A media company must store millions of uploaded videos and serve them to users worldwide. Object, block or file storage, and why not the others?

items: **Why**: it **scales cheaply** for large **unstructured files**, is reached over **HTTP APIs**, and suits **media**, **backups** and **archives**, ideally with a **CDN** for **global delivery**
**Not block**: a **low-latency disk for one VM** → doesn't scale as **shared media storage**
**Not file**: a **shared filesystem for VMs**, which the **web and mobile clients** don't need

check.q: A lift-and-shift app on 8 VMs expects a shared directory, and its database needs a fast local disk. Which storage type for each?

items: **Shared directory → file storage**: many VMs can **mount** it **without the app changing**, which is typical for **lift-and-shift**
**Database disk → block storage**: **low-latency attached volumes**
a.foot: Moving the shared directory to **object storage** later would **scale better** but needs **code changes**.

check.q: A web app behind a managed load balancer went down when its only zone failed, and an attack sent malformed HTTP requests that the network firewall didn't block. What was missing in each case?

items: **Zone failure**: a **load balancer** only helps **availability** if **healthy backend capacity** remains → the backends needed to be **spread across zones**
**Malformed HTTP**: **network firewall rules** filter **connections**, not **HTTP content** → a **WAF** was needed to filter **malicious HTTP requests**
a.foot: **Being managed doesn't mean configured**: **capacity**, **placement** and **filtering** are still **design choices**.

sections.title: Data, messaging, performance and security
sections.summary: Managed data and analytics, streaming and messaging, and operations and security services.

notes.h: Data services by shape and workload
items: **Relational (RDS, Cloud SQL)** → structured transactional data
**NoSQL (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB)** → flexible or high-scale access
**Warehouse (BigQuery, Synapse, Redshift)** → SQL analytics over huge data
**Big-data engines (EMR, Dataproc)** → Hadoop/Spark processing
**Plus** AutoML and data catalogue/integration services

notes.lead: Messaging separates distribution from work ownership.
items: **Streams** → retain ordered event data for processing and replay
**Event routing** → connects producers to interested consumers
**Queue** → distributes work among competing workers
**Pub/sub** → fans out to independent subscribers
notes.foot: Delivery may be repeated: design **idempotent processing** instead of assuming once-only business effects.

items: **Monitoring** → CloudWatch
**Infrastructure as code** → CloudFormation, reproducible environments
**Identity management** → IAM, access control
**Key management** → KMS, encryption
notes.foot: Automation, observability and security **need not be built from scratch**.

terms.def: Buffer distributing work among competing consumers; retries may deliver a task again.
Publish a message once and fan it out to many subscribers (e.g. SNS, Pub/Sub).
Defining cloud resources in versioned templates (CloudFormation, ARM, Deployment Manager) instead of manual setup.
Key Management Service: managed creation, storage and rotation of encryption keys.

check.q: An order event must be processed once by one of 10 worker instances, and also trigger an email, a loyalty update and an analytics record. Queue, pub/sub or both?

items: **Queue** → **distributes the order work** among **competing workers** → each order is **handled by one**
**Pub/sub** → **fans the event out** to **independent subscribers** (**email**, **loyalty**, **analytics**), usually with **one queue per consumer group**
a.foot: **Delivery can repeat** in either case → consumers must be **idempotent**.

check.q: A queue redelivers a payment task after a worker times out, and the customer is charged twice. What is the fix, and why not simply ask for 'exactly-once' delivery?

items: **Fix**: make the **business operation idempotent** → e.g. **record a stable payment identifier** with its **result**, so a **retry returns the recorded outcome** instead of **charging again**
**Why not exactly-once**: **redelivery after a timeout** is **normal in messaging**
You can't rely on **once-only delivery** to guarantee **once-only business effects**

check.q: A team must replay the last 7 days of click events to rebuild a broken analytics view. Would a message queue or a stream suit this, and why?

items: **Stream** → keeps **ordered event data** for a **retention period** → consumers can **reprocess** and **replay** from an **earlier point**
**Queue** → normally **removes a message** once it has been **processed** → nothing to replay

check.q: A team building on managed services plans to add monitoring, identity and encryption 'after launch'. Why is that risky, and what should be in place at launch?

items: **No identity management** → access is likely **too broad**
**No managed key encryption** → **data protection** depends on **ad-hoc handling**
**No monitoring** → **failures go unseen**
**Retrofitting** each later is harder than **defining them in IaC** from **day one**
a.foot: **At launch**: the provider's **managed identity**, **key management** and **monitoring**, **provisioned through IaC** so they **deploy consistently**.

exam_angles.q: Map a cloud-native e-commerce architecture (product browsing, carts, orders, product images, order processing, notifications) onto categories of managed services on one provider, justifying each, and name the decision that most increases lock-in.

items: **Edge** → **managed DNS** and a **load balancer** with a **WAF**
**Compute** → **managed Kubernetes** for the **long-running services**; **FaaS** for **event handlers** such as **image resizing**
**Data** → a **managed relational database** for **orders** (**ACID**); a **NoSQL store** for **carts and sessions**
**Images** → **object storage** with a **CDN**
**Messaging** → a **queue** for **order processing**; **pub/sub** for **notifications**
**Operations and security** → add **monitoring**, **IaC**, **identity management** and **key management** so they are **built in**
a.foot: **Biggest lock-in**: usually **proprietary data and messaging services**, because **data and semantics** don't move as easily as **container images**.

exam_angles.q: A company plans to run on three major providers 'for portability'. Using the idea of overlapping building blocks, assess what will be portable and what will not, and recommend whether to proceed.

items: **Compare by capability categories** such as **managed Kubernetes**, **object storage** and **messaging**, then check each service's **semantics**, **regions** and **limits**
**Portable**: **containers on Kubernetes** keep **packaging and orchestration** portable
**Not portable**: **data**, **identity**, **networking** and **proprietary managed-service APIs** → need separate **migration and integration work**
a.foot: **Proceed only if** a **concrete benefit** (**regulation**, **resilience against a provider**, a **best-of-breed service**) outweighs the cost of **tripled skills and operations**; otherwise use **one provider** with an **exit strategy**.

exam_angles.q: A team must choose storage for VM boot disks, a database's data files, shared engineering files mounted by 20 VMs, and 5 years of backup archives. Recommend a type for each, and say what happens if the team puts everything on block storage to keep things simple.

items: **Boot disks** and **database files** → **block storage**: **low-latency attached volumes**
**Shared engineering files** → **file storage**: **many VMs must mount** them
**Backup archives** → **object storage**: **cheap** and **durable at scale**

sub: The **shared files** can't easily be **mounted by 20 VMs**
**Archives** would **cost much more** than on object storage

exam_angles.q: A CTO says: 'Use managed services everywhere, so availability and security are the provider's job.' Argue for and against, and state what remains the team's responsibility.

sub: **Managed services offload patching**, **scaling**, **backups** and much **availability** work
→ teams spend their effort on **business code**
Tie you to the **provider's SLA**, which doesn't by itself meet an **application SLA**
The team **chooses capacity** and **availability options** such as **multi-zone placement**

a.foot: **Limit lock-in** with **open standards** where it matters and keep an **exit strategy**.
